teaser.text: Experian is an information and software company whose products help organisations decide whom to trust, lend to and serve. Its business becomes clearer when you follow a dollar: customers pay for data, decisions and introductions, while Experian spends to keep those capabilities accurate, secure and useful.

blocks.heading: Where could Experian’s shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: Experian’s weighted case reaches 3,300.14p by October 2029 for a 22% total return, hinging on continued organic growth, margin gains and cash-funded investment and repurchases. For FY27, management guides to 6–8% organic revenue growth and 50 basis points of Benchmark EBIT margin expansion. It expects double-digit Benchmark EPS growth, capital expenditure of 8% of revenue and operating cash flow conversion of at least 90%.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Experian?

paragraphs.text: The bear case combines weaker US mortgage and consumer-credit activity with a prolonged Consumer Services shortfall. Pricing no longer offsets flat volumes, marketplace referrals fail to replace expired contracts, and higher debt and dispute risk compress the multiple. The price falls to 2091.86 GBp by October 2027 and 1833.93 GBp by October 2029.

The bull case requires credit activity to recover, the bank partnership to ramp and Ascend, identity, health and automotive products to become profitable recurring revenue. Stronger cash generation then funds both investment and larger buybacks, while evidence of durable growth lifts the multiple. The price reaches 3759.74 GBp by October 2027 and 5144.07 GBp by October 2029.

paragraphs.text: Management’s free-cash-flow measure is higher than the stricter calculation because it excludes or adds back selected acquisition and exceptional cash movements. Those payments still happened. Stock compensation is another economic cost: it may not consume cash when recorded, but it transfers value to employees through shares and can dilute shareholders.

blocks.heading: How much does Experian pay in dividends per share?

paragraphs.text: The pressure was clearest in FY26. Free cash flow reached US$1,465 million. Dividends were US$590 million and buybacks were US$727 million, leaving little before acquisitions. Acquisitions then required US$692 million. Net debt rose from US$3,737 million to US$5,101 million across the five year-ends. In household terms, Experian earned money after running the business, distributed much of it, bought another business, and borrowed to cover the gap.

blocks.heading: Is Experian's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after running the business and funding necessary investment. In FY26, Benchmark free cash flow was US$1,583 million, while ordinary dividends were US$590 million. The difference could repay debt, fund acquisitions or repurchase shares, which explains why the free-cash-flow yield exceeds the dividend yield.

paragraphs.text: Dividends rise from $0.80 per share in the first base window to $0.88 in the next. They reach $0.96 by October 2029, close to the company’s record of increases and supported by expected earnings growth. The bear case holds DPS at $0.75 because buybacks, acquisitions and leverage compete for cash. The bull case reaches $1.08 if cash conversion and operating leverage improve.

A dispute or privacy setback during October 2028–2029 would add costs while buyback-related leverage limits flexibility. The base case gains support if FY27 growth stays within guidance, margins widen and recurring cash funds both investment and repurchases.

blocks.heading: What has Experian guided for FY27?

paragraphs.text: The promise covers FY27, the year ending 31 March 2027. Reported revenue growth is expected to be 8.0–11.0% at actual exchange rates. Organic growth means sales from the existing business, excluding acquisitions and currency effects; management expects 6.0–8.0%. Acquisitions add sales by bringing new businesses into the group, while exchange rates can make overseas revenue worth more or less when translated into dollars. Organic growth therefore best shows whether existing customers are buying more.

Management also expects Benchmark EBIT margin to expand by 50 basis points. EBIT is operating profit before interest and tax; Benchmark is Experian’s adjusted measure, which excludes selected acquisition, restructuring and other exceptional items. The company expects that revenue growth and a better margin will produce double-digit growth in Benchmark EPS. A buyback can help EPS too, because the same profit is divided among fewer shares, though that does not itself improve sales or efficiency.

blocks.heading: Has Experian kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Experian delivered 8% organic growth and 60 basis points of constant-currency margin expansion in FY26. Organic growth excludes acquisitions, constant currency removes exchange-rate effects, and a basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. That was credible delivery against management’s stated operating promises.

blocks.heading: What is Experian's revenue and profit trend?

paragraphs.text: Revenue grew 10.0% at actual exchange rates. It grew 8.0% at constant exchange rates and 7.0% organically. Currency and acquisitions therefore contributed to the headline result. Organic growth slowed from the March quarter, but management kept its full-year expectations.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in Experian's next results?

paragraphs.text: The next checkpoint is the half-year result on 18 November 2026. North American Consumer Services grew 3% excluding data-breach services in the first quarter, helped by personal loans and insurance while credit cards remained subdued. Because a marketplace depends on lenders wanting customers, weaker lender marketing or acceptance can reduce fees even when consumers are interested.
